prompt: Match each engine to how it acts on the stream.

pairs.right: a slice of new records at each trigger
each record as it arrives, in a cluster
each record as it arrives, inside your own program

right_distractors: each night, over the whole topic

prompt: A team wants to count sales that sit in a PostgreSQL table, with Kafka Streams and nothing else. What stops them?

choices.text: Kafka Streams cannot keep state
choices.why: It keeps state in local stores backed by topics.

choices.text: It reads and writes Kafka topics only
choices.why: Right. Something has to bring the rows into Kafka first, lesson 14's subject.

choices.text: It needs a Flink cluster to run on
choices.why: It runs inside your own program, with no cluster.

choices.text: It is limited to Python
choices.why: It is a Java library.

prompt: How does a Kafka Streams application run on three machines instead of one?

choices.text: You submit it to a cluster with a parallelism of three
choices.why: There is no cluster to submit to; that is Flink's shape.

choices.text: You start three copies of it
choices.why: Right. The copies find each other through Kafka.

choices.text: You raise the number of threads of the broker
choices.why: The broker does not run your application's code.

choices.text: It cannot; it runs on one machine only
choices.why: Scaling is by starting more copies.

prompt: In Kafka Streams, a table kept up to date from a stream, one row per key, is a ___.
Why does `java -cp "$HOME/kafka/libs/*:." SalesPerShop a` need the `:.` at the end of the classpath?

choices.text: It tells Java to run in the background
choices.why: The classpath is where classes are found, not how the process runs.

choices.text: It adds the directory of the .class
choices.why: Right. The Kafka jars are the library; the compiled program is in `.`.

choices.text: It names the state directory
choices.why: The state directory comes from the argument `a`.

choices.text: It expands the `*` before the shell sees it
choices.why: The quotes stop the shell expanding it; Java expands it.

prompt: Why does `sales-per-book` show each book about once, though its count changed many times?

choices.text: The topic is compacted on every write, keeping one record per key
choices.why: Compaction is later and not on every write; the cache is what holds the changes back.

choices.text: The library sends the latest value per key at each commit
choices.why: Right. Changes wait in a cache and only the newest per key leaves, every second here.

choices.text: The console consumer drops a key it has already printed once
choices.why: The console consumer prints whatever is in the topic.

choices.text: Each book was sold only once
choices.why: The counts are in the twenties; each changed many times.

prompt: What does `SalesPerShop` print once its state becomes RUNNING?

choices.text: The counts per shop
choices.why: The counts go to the output topics, not the screen.

choices.text: The offsets it has committed
choices.why: It does not print offsets.

choices.text: The address of its web page
choices.why: Kafka Streams has no web page of its own.

choices.text: The tasks this copy was given
choices.why: Right. One per input partition of each part of the topology.

prompt: The count per book created a `…-repartition` topic and the count per shop did not. Why?

choices.text: Books outnumber shops, and big counts need their own topic
choices.why: The number of keys is not it; the change of key is.

choices.text: Its key changed from shop to book
choices.why: Right. The sales are written back keyed by book so each book's sales meet in one partition.

choices.text: Counts per shop are kept only in memory
choices.why: They have a changelog too.

choices.text: The repartition topic is the backup of the per-book store
choices.why: That is the changelog; the repartition topic carries the sales re-keyed.

prompt: A copy of the application starts on a new machine with an empty state directory. Where do its counts come from?

choices.text: From the changelog topics
choices.why: Right. The changelog is the backup of every store.

choices.text: From the output topics, which hold the latest counts
choices.why: Output topics are for readers; restoring uses the changelog.

choices.text: From the other copy, over the network, directly
choices.why: Copies never talk to each other directly; Kafka is between them.

choices.text: Nowhere: it counts from zero
choices.why: Starting from zero would lose every count; the changelog prevents it.

prompt: With two copies of `SalesPerShop` running, how many tasks does each copy hold?
What happened to copy `a` when copy `b` started?

choices.text: It stopped, because two copies cannot share a group
choices.why: Sharing a group is exactly how the copies divide the work.

choices.text: It kept all six tasks and `b` waited
choices.why: The group rebalanced and moved half of them.

choices.text: It rebalanced and kept half the tasks
choices.why: Right. Its own lines show the state going back to REBALANCING.

choices.text: It copied its stores to `b` over the network
choices.why: A moved task restores from the changelog, not from the other copy.

prompt: Why does the lesson change two sizes in Flink's `config.yaml`?

choices.text: Flink refuses to start with its defaults on Java 21
choices.why: It starts; the defaults are simply too large for this machine.

choices.text: The defaults take most of the VM's memory
choices.why: Right. 1.6 GB and 1.7 GB before Kafka has anything; a gigabyte each is plenty.

choices.text: To make the web page answer on localhost
choices.why: That is the other change, `bind-address`, not the sizes.

choices.text: To give the Kafka connector room to load
choices.why: The connector is a jar in `lib`; the sizes are about the processes.

prompt: What does the `2.2` in `flink-sql-connector-kafka-5.0.0-2.2.jar` say?

choices.text: The Scala version it was built with
choices.why: Flink's Scala version is the `2.12` in the archive's name.

choices.text: The Kafka version it talks to
choices.why: The connector packs its own Kafka client; 2.2 is not a Kafka version here.

choices.text: Its second patch release
choices.why: The connector's own version is 5.0.0.

choices.text: The Flink version it is built for
choices.why: Right. Version 5.0.0 of the connector, for Flink 2.2.

prompt: The first Flink job ran for ten seconds and wrote no window, while Spark wrote six from the same sales. What was different?

choices.text: Flink's watermark waits for the slowest partition, and partition 2 had nothing
choices.why: Right. An empty partition has no watermark, so none could close a window until it was declared idle.

choices.text: Flink's windows are longer than Spark's by default, so the first one had not closed yet
choices.why: Both were five minutes, written in the query.

choices.text: Flink only writes a window when the job is stopped, which nobody had done yet
choices.why: After the fix it wrote six while running.

choices.text: The JSON format could not read `at`
choices.why: After one more SET line the same table produced the counts.

prompt: The Flink setting that lets a quiet partition stop holding back the watermark is `table.exec.source.___-timeout`.
In `sales.sql`, what does the `CREATE TABLE sales` statement do to Kafka?

choices.text: It creates the topic `sales` with three partitions and the JSON format
choices.why: The topic already existed; the statement only describes it to Flink.

choices.text: Nothing; it tells Flink how to read the topic as a table
choices.why: Right. Columns, watermark and connector settings, all on Flink's side.

choices.text: It deletes and recreates the topic
choices.why: Nothing in the topic was touched; the sales were still read.

choices.text: It registers a schema in the registry
choices.why: No registry is involved; the format is plain JSON.

prompt: Put the steps of getting Flink's first windows in the order the lesson takes them.
items: Submit sales.sql with the SQL client
Read the output topic and find nothing
Submit again and read six windows

prompt: Why does Flink send a barrier through the stream instead of letting each operator save its state on its own clock?

choices.text: So the snapshot is one consistent point
choices.why: Right. Otherwise a restore would count some sales twice or not at all.

choices.text: To stop the stream while the snapshot is taken
choices.why: The records keep flowing; that is the point of the barrier.

choices.text: To tell the sink to write its rows
choices.why: Windows are written when the watermark closes them, not at barriers.

choices.text: To measure lag
choices.why: Barriers carry no measurement; they mark a point in the stream.

prompt: Which statement about checkpoints and savepoints matches the section?

choices.text: Savepoints are taken by Flink every ten seconds and deleted when replaced
choices.why: That describes checkpoints.

choices.text: Checkpoints keep only offsets, savepoints keep state as well
choices.why: Both are the same kind of snapshot, offsets and state.

choices.text: A savepoint is taken when you ask, and kept until you delete it
choices.why: Right. Checkpoints are Flink's, for crashes; savepoints are yours, for planned stops.

choices.text: Only a savepoint can restore a job
choices.why: A checkpoint is what restores a job after a crash.

prompt: After the restore, the job wrote 09:30 with 24 sales and 09:35 with 14. Why does that prove the savepoint was used?

choices.text: Because the job id stayed the same
choices.why: The restored job has a new id.

choices.text: Because both numbers equal the topic's partition count
choices.why: The topic has three partitions; that is unrelated.

choices.text: Because Flink always writes the last two windows on start
choices.why: No such rule; what was written depended on restored state.

choices.text: Only 2 sales were read, but the counts include the 13 from before
choices.why: Right. The earlier counts came back from the savepoint, and the source resumed from its offsets.

prompt: Roughly how many gigabytes did the Kafka node and Flink's two processes hold together? (Answer to one decimal.)
A team already runs Spark for its nightly jobs and needs a dashboard that may lag by a few seconds. What does the section suggest?

choices.text: Install Flink, because it is the fastest of the three engines
choices.why: Speed is looked at last, and a few seconds is within Spark's reach.

choices.text: Structured Streaming on the Spark they already run
choices.why: Right. Same cluster, same people, almost nothing new to operate.

choices.text: Kafka Streams in a new Java service
choices.why: Possible, but it adds a service and a language the team does not run.

choices.text: A batch every second
choices.why: That is the shrinking batch of lesson 1, not a stream.

prompt: Ponto Final's stock count per book lives inside the service that answers the website. Why does the section read that as a Kafka Streams shape?

choices.text: Kafka Streams is the only engine that can count per key
choices.why: All three count per key; the reason is where the state lives.

choices.text: Only Kafka Streams has exactly-once
choices.why: Each can reach it under conditions; that is not the argument.

choices.text: The state is per key and kept by the app, with no engine to run beside it
choices.why: Right. The service already reads Kafka; the library adds the table to it.

choices.text: It is the cheapest per message
choices.why: Cost per message is not the section's argument.

prompt: A Flink job reading a topic of twelve partitions writes no windows; eleven partitions receive sales and one has been empty since a shop closed. What fixes it without losing late sales from the other eleven?

choices.text: Lower the watermark bound to zero
choices.why: The bound is not the problem; the empty partition has no watermark at all.

choices.text: Restart the job from a savepoint
choices.why: The empty partition would still hold the watermark back.

choices.text: An idle timeout, so the empty partition stops counting
choices.why: Right. The other eleven keep their own watermarks, late sales included.

choices.text: Switch to processing time
choices.why: That would put late sales in the wrong windows, lesson 9's warning.

prompt: Which of these would show up in `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --list` while it runs?

choices.text: Spark Structured Streaming
choices.why: Lesson 12's list was empty: Spark assigns partitions itself and keeps offsets in its checkpoint.

choices.text: Kafka Streams
choices.why: Right. Its copies are members of a group named after the application id.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: Kafka Streams relies on a consumer group to divide its tasks.

choices.text: The till, `tills.py`, that feeds all three
choices.why: A producer writes; it joins no consumer group.
